582.title: Four kinds of samana
582.hook: Cunda the smith asks how many kinds of wandering seekers there are
582.howItsDone: In Buddhist communities the monastic code sets standards for those who wear the robe, and lay supporters help hold monastics to them; Cunda's poem is one text Buddhists turn to on telling sincere seekers from pretenders.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saddha, faith the seed, and your line, plant one seed you can't see. Today a craftsman asks a sharp question about the people who wear the robe.

A news story breaks about a religious leader who did something terrible, and at the dinner table someone says: see, they're all the same. It's an old sentence, and a sharp one. The fifth poem of the Sutta Nipata takes it on. A metalworker named Cunda, the smith's son, asks the Buddha: how many kinds of samanas are there in the world? A samana is a wandering seeker, someone who has left home for the spiritual life. Cunda wants to know how to tell them apart.
screen: `THEY'RE ALL THE SAME.` → `CUNDA THE SMITH ASKS.` → `HOW DO YOU TELL THEM APART?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers: four, and no fifth. The first has conquered the path: beyond doubt, free of the arrow, delighting in freedom, a guide for the world. The second shows the path: knows the highest as the highest, explains it and lays it out right here, cutting through other people's doubts. The third lives the path: well restrained, mindful, walking the well-taught way, doing no harm. The fourth defiles the path. He wears the same robe as the good ones and looks the part. But he's pushy, deceitful, unrestrained, a fraud in disguise, and he spoils the families who trust him. The poem calls him chaff. Then comes the answer to the dinner table. A lay follower who has heard and understood this sees the fourth kind for what he is, and doesn't lose trust in the others because of him. How could the pure and the impure be the same? Notice the order. Tradition reads the first as the Buddha himself. But the second, the one who shows, is any good teacher who explains clearly and clears up doubt. You don't have to have arrived to point the way well. And the warning in the fourth is honest: the robe alone proves nothing. A poem that names its own frauds this plainly is taking trust seriously.
screen: `THE ONE WHO HAS CONQUERED THE PATH` · `THE ONE WHO SHOWS IT, THE ONE WHO LIVES IT` · `THE ONE WHO DEFILES IT` · `ONE FRAUD DOESN'T MAKE THEM ALL` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SHOWS.`

segments.voice: Remember someone who showed you a good path, a teacher, a coach, a grandparent, a friend who explained something kindly: not someone who had it all figured out, just someone who pointed clearly. See their face and thank them silently, then rest with the breath.
samana. Cunda's question: the one who conquers the path, the one who shows it, the one who lives it, and the one who wears the robe and defiles it. Today's word.
Your line: the one who shows. One fraud doesn't make them all the same. Until tomorrow.

583.title: Downfall
583.hook: a shining visitor asks, again and again: and what is the next cause of downfall?
583.howItsDone: The Parabhava Sutta is among the protective discourses chanted in Theravada communities, and it is often taught to lay Buddhists as practical advice on family, money and friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samana, Cunda's four kinds of seeker, and your line, the one who shows. Today, the opposite direction: how people slide.

Nobody wakes up one morning and decides to wreck their life. It goes slower than that. A habit here, a skipped call to a parent there, a little more money spent than earned, a little more pride than the situation needed. Years later, it adds up. The sixth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a slow-motion map of that slide. Late at night, a shining deity lights up the grove where the Buddha is staying, asks one question, then keeps coming back with the same follow-up: that's one. Tell me the next.
screen: `NOBODY DECIDES TO FALL.` → `A SHINING VISITOR AT NIGHT.` → `TELL ME THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Parabhava Sutta, the discourse on downfall, or decline. It opens simply: the one who rises is easy to know, and the one who falls is easy to know. Whoever loves the good teaching rises; whoever hates it falls. Then the visitor asks for the next cause, and the next, about a dozen in all. Some sound ancient, addressed to a man of that time. But many land today. Keeping company with bad people and liking their ways. Loving sleep, loving crowds, never making an effort, quick to anger. Being able to support your aging mother and father, and not doing it. Lying to a holy person to deceive them. Having plenty of wealth and good food, and eating it alone. Being proud of your family, your money or your name, and looking down on your own relatives. Drinking, gambling, chasing affairs, and losing what you earn. Putting a reckless spender in charge of your affairs. Having little and wanting a throne. Notice what's barely on the list: ritual. Apart from the first verse, about the teaching itself, and a few on sloth and appetite, the causes are ways of treating people: parents, relatives, the hungry, the trusting. Downfall here is mostly relational. And one quiet detail: the wealthy person isn't condemned for being wealthy, only for eating alone. The poem closes: the wise, seeing these causes of downfall clearly, take the safe road.
screen: `THE ONE WHO RISES IS EASY TO KNOW` · `TELL ME THE NEXT CAUSE` · `PARENTS, RELATIVES, THE HUNGRY` · `NOT RICH: RICH AND EATING ALONE` · then, large: `CAUSES OF DOWNFALL.`

segments.voice: Go through the list quietly, bad company, too much sleep, a parent who needs a call, a meal not shared, pride in front of family, money leaking away, and notice which sits closest to your life right now, without judging yourself. Then picture one small step away from it, a call, a shared plate, an early night, and hold that picture for a few breaths.
Downfall. The Parabhava Sutta: about a dozen ways a person slowly falls, almost all of them about how we treat the people around us. Today's word.
Your line: causes of downfall. Most of them are about how we treat each other. Day five hundred eighty-three, done.

584.title: By deeds
584.hook: a man shouts 'outcast!' at the Buddha, and gets a question back
584.carry: what someone does, not where they're from
584.howItsDone: The Vasala Sutta is chanted as one of the protective discourses in Theravada communities, and Buddhists speaking about dignity and caste quote its line, not by birth, by deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the slow slide, and your line, causes of downfall. Today, an insult shouted across a doorway, and a calm reply.

Morning in the city of Savatthi. In one house a brahmin named Aggika Bharadvaja has his sacred fire burning and his offerings laid out, everything ready and pure. Down the street with his alms bowl comes the Buddha. To this man, at this moment, a shaven-headed wanderer near his fire is a kind of pollution. So he shouts. Stop there, shaveling! Stop there, you wretched monk! Stop there, outcast! There are two easy moves next: shout back, or walk away hurt. The Buddha does neither.
screen: `A SACRED FIRE, READY AND PURE.` → `STOP THERE, OUTCAST!` → `NEITHER SHOUTING NOR LEAVING.`

segments.voice: He asks a question. Do you know, brahmin, what an outcast is, or what makes someone one? The brahmin, maybe surprised, says: no, I don't. Teach me. So the Buddha does, in verse. In the brahmin's mouth, vasala, outcast, is an insult about birth: a word for someone low, someone whose presence stains. The Buddha keeps the word and changes what earns it. Whoever is angry and holds grudges is an outcast. Whoever harms living beings. Whoever steals, or borrows money and then denies the debt. Whoever lies as a witness. Whoever is able to support aging parents and doesn't. Whoever strikes or insults their family. Whoever does wrong and hopes no one will find out. Whoever praises themselves and looks down on others. Then he tells of Matanga, a candala's son, born into a group his society kept at the bottom, who became so renowned that nobles and brahmins came to serve him. His birth didn't stop him. Then the line: not by birth is one an outcast, not by birth is one a brahmin. By deeds one becomes an outcast; by deeds one becomes a brahmin. And look at the scene. The list is long, and the man who just shouted is standing right there, angry, looking down on someone. The Buddha never says so. He describes it, and lets the brahmin find himself in it. At the end, the brahmin asks to become a follower.
screen: `DO YOU KNOW WHAT AN OUTCAST IS?` · `ANGRY, CRUEL, LOOKING DOWN ON OTHERS` · `MATANGA, BORN LOW, HONORED HIGH` · `NOT BY BIRTH: BY DEEDS` · then, large: `BY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone people tend to overlook or look down on, the person who empties the bins, the new kid, the neighbor nobody greets, and see them clearly. Recall one good deed you've seen them do, or could imagine them doing, and let that deed, not their place, be what you see.
By deeds. The Buddha's answer to the brahmin who called him an outcast: no one is low or noble by birth, only by what they do. Today's word.
Your line: what someone does, not where they're from. Birth was never the measure. See you tomorrow.

585.title: Kindness, read again
585.hook: the loving-kindness discourse, read whole, start to finish
585.carry: as a mother her only child
585.howItsDone: The Karaniya Metta Sutta is chanted in Pali in Theravada temples and homes, often from memory, as one of the protective chants called paritta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: by deeds, and your line, what someone does, not where they're from. Today, a text you've met before, read the whole way through.
screen: `WHAT SOMEONE DOES, NOT WHERE THEY'RE FROM.`

segments.voice: A radio edit trims a song down. Then one day the full album version plays, with the verse the radio left out, and the same song is suddenly bigger. More than a year ago, in the first months of this path, there were days on loving-kindness, metta, and its picture of a mother and her child. Now, reading the Sutta Nipata in order, the poem itself arrives, the eighth piece in the book. Ten short verses, heard start to finish, to notice the shape.
screen: `THE ALBUM VERSION.` → `THE EIGHTH POEM IN THE BOOK.` → `START TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: The poem moves in three steps. First, how to live. Before any wishing, it describes a person: capable, upright, gentle, easy to speak to, not proud, content, not weighed down by busyness, calm in the senses, not greedy with families, doing nothing the wise would criticize. Kindness starts as a way of behaving. Second, the wishes. May all beings be happy and at ease. Weak or strong, long or short, big or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born: may all beings be happy. Let no one deceive another or look down on anyone anywhere, or wish harm on anyone in anger. Then the image at the center: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so let one cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. It's the boundlessness being compared: a love that doesn't measure. Third, the reach. Kindness spreading above, below and all around, without obstruction, hatred or enmity. Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake, keep this mindfulness. This, the poem says, is called a divine way of living, right here. And the last verse turns. It ends not on love but on seeing: not grasping at views, having clear vision, letting go of greed for sense pleasures, such a one won't be born again into a womb. Kindness, in this poem, isn't only warm. It's a path to waking up.
screen: `FIRST, HOW TO LIVE` · `THEN THE WISHES: ALL BEINGS` · `A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD` · `ABOVE, BELOW, ALL AROUND` · then, large: `AS A MOTHER HER ONLY CHILD.`

segments.voice: Say the wishes slowly, in the poem's order: may all beings be happy and at ease, the weak and the strong, the seen and the unseen, the near and the far, those born and those yet to be born. Then picture the mother bent over her only child, and let that same unmeasured care spread above you, below you, all around. If you know the Pali, you can chant it instead.
Kindness. Metta, as the poem lays it out whole: a way of living, a set of wishes for all beings, and a boundless heart spreading in every direction. Today's word.
Your line: as a mother her only child. A heart that doesn't measure. That's day five hundred eighty-five.

586.title: Two spirits talk
586.hook: two mountain spirits check the Buddha's character before they go to meet him
586.howItsDone: Buddhist texts encourage people to examine a teacher's conduct and speech over time before placing trust in them, and on uposatha days, the holy days of the lunar month, lay Buddhists may visit a temple, keep extra precepts and hear teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the kindness poem, whole, and your line, as a mother her only child. Today, two spirits on a mountain, gossiping.

Before you hire someone, you call their references. Before you try a new doctor, you ask a friend: is she any good? Not her diploma. Her. Does she listen? Is she honest? The ninth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a reference check, done by two yakkhas, nature spirits of the hills. It's the fifteenth night of the month, a holy day. One spirit, Satagira, says to his friend: tonight's a special night. Let's go see the teacher Gotama. And his friend Hemavata, from the Himalaya, says: wait. First, tell me about him.
screen: `CALL THE REFERENCES.` → `A HOLY NIGHT ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `WAIT. TELL ME ABOUT HIM.`

segments.voice: Hemavata's questions come in a steady rhythm, and Satagira answers every one. Is his mind well disposed toward all beings? It is. Does he master his reactions to what he likes and what he doesn't? He does. Does he take what isn't given? He doesn't. Is he restrained toward living things, never careless, never neglecting meditation? He is. Does he lie? Speak harshly? Carry tales between people? Chatter about nothing? No, no, no and no. His words, Satagira says, are measured and full of sense. Is he free from craving, his mind clear, with the eye that sees the truth? Yes. Notice what Hemavata doesn't ask. Not: can he do miracles? Not: how famous is he? Not even: what does he teach? Every question is about character: how he treats beings, how he speaks, whether his mind is steady. That's the test the poem sets for a teacher. And notice Satagira. He doesn't exaggerate or sell. He answers honestly, one question at a time, and in doing it he speaks well of someone good. Then the two spirits go down the mountain and ask the Buddha their own questions. What does the world arise in? In six, he says: the six senses. At the end, the spirits decide to travel from village to village and mountain to mountain, honoring the Buddha and the teaching. A good reputation, carried by a friend's honest words, became a journey.
screen: `WAIT: TELL ME ABOUT HIM FIRST` · `HOW HE TREATS BEINGS, HOW HE SPEAKS` · `CHARACTER, NOT MIRACLES` · `AN HONEST FRIEND'S GOOD WORD` · then, large: `THEY SPOKE WELL OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Choose someone you respect, a teacher, a coworker, a relative, and quietly ask Hemavata's questions about them: are they kind to people, do they tell the truth, do they stay out of gossip? Let honest answers come, not flattery, and notice which ones make you glad.
yakkha. Hemavata asks about the Buddha's character, Satagira answers honestly, and a good word, well spoken, sends them down the mountain. Today's word.
Your line: they spoke well of him. An honest good word can start a journey. Until tomorrow.

587.title: Faith the best wealth
587.hook: a fierce spirit orders the Buddha in and out, then threatens him with a riddle
587.howItsDone: The taming of Alavaka is one of the episodes recalled in the Jayamangala Gatha, a verse chant of the Buddha's victories recited in Theravada temples and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two mountain spirits checking references, and your line, they spoke well of him. Today, a much less friendly spirit.

Get out. So the Buddha gets up and goes out. Come in. So he comes back in. Get out. He goes. Come in. He comes. The spirit is a yakkha named Alavaka, and this is his house, and he's testing how far he can push this calm visitor. The fourth time he says get out, the Buddha says: no, friend, I won't. Do what you have to do. And Alavaka makes his threat. I'll ask you a question. If you can't answer it, I'll scramble your mind, or split your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you across the Ganges.
screen: `GET OUT. COME IN.` → `THE FOURTH TIME: NO.` → `ANSWER, OR ELSE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's reply is calm. In all the world, he says, I see no one who could scramble my mind or split my heart. But ask whatever you like. Notice what he did first. Three times, he went along. Not out of fear, the commentary says, but to soften a hard mind with gentleness. Only the fourth time, when obeying would have been just a game, did he say no. Then the questions come, in verse. What is the best wealth a person has? Faith, the Buddha answers, saddha, trust in what is good. What, practiced well, brings happiness? The teaching. What is the sweetest of all tastes? Truth. Living how is the best life? Living with wisdom. Then the deeper ones. How does one cross the flood? By faith. How does one cross the sea? By care, by not being careless. How does one get past suffering? By effort. How does one become pure? By wisdom. Why faith? One way to hear it: look at what the threat was. Alavaka could take your mind, your body, your life. But trust in something good is a wealth that's still yours while you're being threatened. It's what lets you answer calmly. At the end, the fierce spirit says, in words close to yesterday's spirits, that he'll travel from village to village, honoring the one who is fully awake. Theravada chants still recall the taming of Alavaka.
screen: `THREE TIMES YES, THE FOURTH TIME NO` · `NO ONE CAN SPLIT MY HEART` · `THE BEST WEALTH IS FAITH` · `CROSS THE FLOOD BY TRUST` · then, large: `FAITH THE BEST WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Picture a small threat arriving, a demanding message, a tense meeting, a sharp relative, and notice any jolt in the chest. Breathe out slowly and picture yourself answering the way the Buddha did, not shrinking, not striking back: ask what they want, and answer plainly. Let your shoulders drop, and notice what's still yours.
saddha. The Buddha's first answer to the threatening spirit Alavaka: trust in what is good is a person's best wealth. Today's word.
Your line: answer once, calmly and plainly. Some wealth stays yours, even under threat. Day five hundred eighty-seven, done.

588.title: The body as it is
588.hook: walking, standing, sitting, lying down: a poem that looks at the body plainly
588.howItsDone: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist meditation, taught especially to monastics; teachers present it as a way to loosen vanity and craving, not to cultivate disgust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saddha, the best wealth, and your line, answer once, calmly and plainly. Today ends the week, with the most ordinary thing you own.

Some days you catch yourself in a shop window and think: not bad. Other days the bathroom mirror at seven in the morning says something else entirely. Plenty of people swing between those two, pride and dislike, about the same body, sometimes within the same hour. Phones add filters to fix one side; ads sell the other. The eleventh poem of the Sutta Nipata asks for something rarer than either. Not a better body, not a worse opinion of it. Just a clear look.
screen: `THE SHOP WINDOW: NOT BAD.` → `THE MIRROR AT 7 A.M.` → `SOMETHING RARER: A CLEAR LOOK.`

segments.voice: The poem starts with movement. Walking or standing, sitting or lying down, bending and stretching: that's what a body does. Then it looks inside, the way an honest anatomy lesson would. Bones and sinews, wrapped in skin and flesh. A belly, a liver, a heart, lungs, kidneys. Things the skin covers, so they aren't seen as they are. Then it looks at what comes out: tears, sweat, the things that leave the body every day. Some listeners find this part uncomfortable, and that's worth noticing. The poem isn't trying to make anyone ashamed. Its last lines name the point. Whoever thinks highly of themselves because of a body like this, or looks down on someone else because of theirs, what is that, the poem asks, except not seeing? So it cuts two ways at once. Against vanity: this body is not a trophy. Against contempt: no one is lesser because of theirs. What's left is steady and kind: a body that walks and bends and breathes, seen plainly. This week was about seeing plainly, too. Four kinds of seekers, and a robe that proves nothing. A slow slide, told cause by cause. Not by birth, by deeds. The kindness poem, whole. Two spirits checking character. A threat answered with calm. Each time, the poem looks past the surface, a robe, a birth, a threat, to what is actually there.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING` · `BONES, SINEWS, SKIN, HEART` · `NO PRIDE, NO CONTEMPT` · `A WEEK OF LOOKING PAST THE SURFACE` · then, large: `AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Feel your feet, your hands, the weight in the chair, the breath moving the belly, and somewhere inside, a heart working without asking for thanks. If a judgment comes, too heavy, too tired, not bad, name it, judging, and come back to the plain feeling: warm here, tight there, moving, breathing, a body as it is.
Kaya, the body, in Pali. The Sutta Nipata's eleventh poem: seeing the body plainly, so there's no ground for pride in your own or contempt for anyone else's. Today's word.
Your line: as it is. No trophy, and nothing to look down on. See you tomorrow.
